title: Bhagiratha and the rest of us
hookLine: a king whose grandfather and father both failed to bring the Ganga down doesn't stop, and Patanjali says why that matters
carry: faith and intensity, not talent, bring you near
tomorrow: an elephant's strength runs out. who comes?
last: SAMADHI — THE MIND GATHERED ON ONE SEED.

lines: A GRANDFATHER TRIED. A FATHER TRIED.
cards: You met Bhagiratha on day one hundred fifteen: the king who brought the Ganga down from heaven. Here's the part before.

Sixty thousand of his ancestors, the sons of King Sagara, lay burned to ash by the sage Kapila, and only the Ganga's water could free them. His grandfather, Anshuman, tried for the rest of his life and died without her.
His father, Dilipa, worried over it and died without an answer. Nobody in that family was born able to do this. Then it was Bhagiratha's turn.

teach.h: ARMS RAISED, ONE MEAL A MONTH.
teach.b: In Valmiki's Ramayana, he hands his kingdom to his ministers and goes to Gokarna to practice tapas: arms raised, fires around him, eating once a month, for a very long time.
Brahma grants the river, but warns that only Shiva can bear her fall. So Bhagiratha begins again, standing on the tip of one toe for a year, until Shiva agrees.
In Hindi, a vast, stubborn effort is still called a Bhagiratha effort. Patanjali has words for what Bhagiratha had.

Sutra 1.19 admits that a few beings reach deep absorption by their very nature; the commentator Vyasa adds that their state wears off, so they aren't the goal. Sutra 1.20 turns to everyone else: five things come first.
Shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real. Virya, energy. Smriti, memory, keeping the aim in view.
Samadhi, the gathering. Prajna, wisdom. Talent isn't on the list, and each can be grown.
Sutra 1.21: it is near for those whose urgency is intense. And 1.22 grades even that: mild, medium, intense.
This is a real Hindu conviction, and the stories keep telling it: the goal isn't reserved for the born-holy.

Many teachers read these sutras this way: how near you are depends on how much you care, not on what you were born with. Today, it might be a grandmother you assume was born devout, who in fact just kept getting up early.

how: In Hindi a vast, stubborn effort is still called a Bhagiratha effort, and yoga teachers often present shraddha, virya, smriti, samadhi and prajna as qualities anyone can cultivate, pointing to sutra 1.21 to say that sincere intensity matters more than natural gifts.

o: faith: a settled trust that the path is real
blind belief that asks no questions at all
a vow of obedience to one's teacher

p: memory: keeping the aim in view

s: Bhagiratha succeeded because he was born with special powers
his grandfather and father both failed. Valmiki tells of his long tapas, then a second round to win Shiva.
for everyone else, the goal comes after faith, energy, memory, absorption and wisdom
Patanjali says the goal is near for those with intense urgency

games.q: Bhagiratha's grandfather and father both failed before him. by Patanjali's sutras, what decides how near the goal is?
o: the family you were born into.
faith, and the intensity of your wanting and effort.
games.why: 1.20 lists faith, energy, memory, gathering and wisdom, none of them inborn, and 1.21 says the goal is near for the intense. Bhagiratha is that sutra in a story.

practice: If you pray, sit with a name of God you love; if you don't, with the breath. Touch the five, a few breaths each: faith, trusting that this sitting counts; energy, lengthen the spine and wake the body; memory, recall why you came.
Then gather on the name or the breath. For wisdom, notice without judging how intense your wanting is today, mild, medium or intense. Any of them is a fine place to start.

wordCard.voice: Shraddha, faith, a settled trust that the path is real, the first of the five in sutra 1.20. Bhagiratha kept it after two generations of his family had failed.

orig.note: Sanskrit śraddhā: faith, trust. the first of the five that come before samadhi in 1.20.

carryVoice: Your line: faith and intensity, not talent, bring you near. Tomorrow, an elephant whose strength runs out. Day four hundred thirty-five.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 42–43 (Anshuman and Dilipa fail; Bhagiratha's tapas at Gokarna; standing on his toe for Shiva; the Ganga's descent), sarga numbers vary by edition
Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.19–1.22 (the born-free; faith, energy, memory, samadhi, wisdom; mild, medium, intense)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.19 (the videhas and prakriti-layas return)
